title: Francis Xavier (1506–1552)
hook: he baptizes across India and Japan and dies off the coast of China

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jesuits: a failed pilgrimage, an offer to the pope, and a motto. Your line was for the greater glory. Which choice served more? Today one of Ignatius's roommates is sent east. Day eight hundred fifty.

The ending comes first. A small island off the coast of China, a hut, a fever, and a man waiting for a boat that never comes. He has a plan to slip into the mainland, where foreigners are forbidden, and he's been told it could cost him his freedom or his life. He's still waiting when he dies. Behind him lie India, the islands of the spice trade, and Japan. He was once a promising young teacher in Paris, rooming with an older student who kept asking him an uncomfortable question. The older student was Ignatius. The young teacher was Francis Xavier.
screen: `AN ISLAND OFF CHINA.` → `A BOAT THAT NEVER COMES.` → `ONCE A TEACHER IN PARIS.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Tradition says Ignatius kept repeating one line of the Gospel to his ambitious roommate, from Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "For what doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his own soul?" Xavier wanted a career. That question slowly turned him around. Second, the sending. When the king of Portugal asked for missionaries for India, another Jesuit was chosen and fell ill. Xavier was sent instead, almost overnight. He never saw Ignatius again. Third, the road. In India he walked the coast, taught children prayers in their own language, and baptized. Then he went on, to the islands, to Japan. In Japan he learned that his ragged clothes made people take him less seriously, not more, and he changed his approach. Then China. He never reached the mainland. Fourth, the letters. Xavier wrote long letters home to his brothers in Europe, and they were copied and read aloud. In one he says he wishes he could run through the universities of Europe shouting to the students about the people waiting for someone to come. It's also true that his travels went by Portuguese ships, inside a trading empire, and that empire's record is a hard one. The Church names him a patron of the missions. His line, if he had one, was always further.
screen: `WHAT DOTH IT PROFIT A MAN?` · `SENT IN ANOTHER MAN'S PLACE.` · `INDIA, THE ISLANDS, JAPAN.` · `LETTERS READ ALOUD IN EUROPE.` · then, large: `ALWAYS FURTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write to someone far away. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone at a distance: another city, another country, or just far from you in the ways that count. Picture their face. What would they be glad to hear from you? Start a message. A few lines are enough. Don't send it yet if you'd rather wait; just begin. If you pray, you can pray for them as you write. If you don't, simply keep them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Francis Xavier. Ignatius's roommate from Paris, sent east to India and Japan, who died on an island off the coast of China, still going further.
Your line: always further. Today, send the message you started, or go one step past where you'd usually stop for someone: one more call, one more mile, one more try. Day eight hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Francis Xavier's feast, and he is honored as a patron of missions; his remains are venerated in Goa, India.

what it means: an ambitious young teacher turned around by one question, sent east in another man's place.
what a scholar hears: his letters were copied and read aloud across Europe, and historians weigh how his mission traveled inside a trading empire.
